payload.stem: A seed company states that each of its seeds germinates with probability $0.3$, independently of other seeds. options.why: A trial uses a different number of digits than the $4$ seeds in the scenario, so the simulated event is not the one asked about.

options.text: The digits $0$ through $2$ represent that a seed germinates and $3$ through $9$ that it is not; each trial reads $4$ random digits and records whether at least $2$ of them are in the first group, repeated for many trials
options.why: The probability that a seed germinates is $0.3$, so $3$ of the $10$ equally likely digits represent it; one trial has $4$ seeds, and the event counted is at least $2$.

options.text: The digits $0$ through $2$ represent that a seed germinates and $3$ through $9$ that it is not; each trial reads $4$ random digits and records whether exactly $2$ of them are in the first group, repeated for many trials
options.why: Counts a different event: the scenario asks for at least $2$, not exactly $2$.

options.text: The digits $0$ through $4$ represent that a seed germinates and $5$ through $9$ that it is not; each trial reads $4$ random digits and records whether at least $2$ of them are in the first group, repeated for many trials

payload.stem: A teacher wants to know whether a review session changes test scores. Each student's score is recorded on a test before the session and on a similar test after the session, and the difference is found as before minus after. The teacher suspects that the review session raises the mean score. Let $\mu_d$ be the mean difference (before minus after), in points, for all students. Which of the following pairs of hypotheses should be tested?

options.text: $H_0: \bar{x}_d = 0$ and $H_a: \bar{x}_d < 0$
options.why: Writes the hypotheses about a sample mean, but hypotheses are always about the population parameter.

options.text: $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ and $H_a: \mu_d \ne 0$
options.why: Writes a two-sided alternative although the suspicion has a direction.

options.text: $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ and $H_a: \mu_d > 0$
options.why: Reverses the direction of the alternative hypothesis relative to the suspicion. The direction of a mean difference follows the order of subtraction in its definition.

options.text: $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ and $H_a: \mu_d < 0$
options.why: The parameter is the mean difference (before minus after), in points, for all students; the null hypothesis states the claimed value and the alternative matches the suspicion and the order of subtraction in the definition.

payload.stem: A $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean number of hours of sleep that students at a university get each night is constructed from a random sample of $49$ students using a one-sample $t$-interval. A researcher then constructs a $90\%$ confidence interval from a new random sample of $16$ students. Assume that the sample standard deviation is the same for both samples and that the conditions for inference are met. Which of the following statements about the width of the new interval compared with the original interval is correct?

options.text: The new interval will have the same width as the original interval
options.why: Assumes the two effects cancel exactly, but the new margin of error is about $1.53$ times the original margin of error.

options.text: The new interval will be narrower than the original interval
options.why: Lets the lower confidence level dominate, but the new margin of error is about $1.53$ times the original margin of error, so the smaller sample size has the larger effect and the interval is wider.

options.text: The new interval will be wider than the original interval
options.why: The smaller sample size has the larger effect: the new margin of error is about $1.53$ times the original margin of error, so the interval is wider.

options.text: The relative width of the new interval cannot be determined without knowing the value of the sample standard deviation
